meta.title: Evaluating Agentic Workflows
meta.thesis: Evaluating Agentic Workflows is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: A multi-step ticket agent must be judged on tool choices, state updates, and final answer quality. By the end, they should be able to build or review agent workflow evaluation trace with step-level assertions, measure task success with correct intermediate actions, and catch the failure where the final answer looks right while the agent took unsafe or wasteful steps.

mentalMap.title: Evaluating Agentic Workflows: mental map
mentalMap.caption: Evaluate agentic workflows by final success, trace behavior, tool safety, retrieval, cost, and recovery rather than final prose alone.
mentalMap.oneLineThesis: Agent workflow evaluation must score the path because tool calls, retries, approvals, and retrieval can fail while the final answer sounds fine.

modules.title: Final text is only one output
modules.sub: The workflow path can be wrong even when prose is polished.
modules.summary: Agent eval starts from the full run trace.
objectives: Explain why final-answer scoring is insufficient.

blocks.title: An agent answer has a supply chain

spans.text: Problem anchor: a refund agent writes a correct-looking apology but skipped policy retrieval and called the refund tool without approval. Final prose alone would pass; workflow eval fails it.
Agentic evals should inspect route, tools, arguments, retrieved evidence, approvals, retries, cost, latency, and final response.
For each user-visible answer, identify the internal steps that must be true.

blocks.analogy: The final answer is the receipt; the trace is the kitchen camera.

spans.text: The trace shows no retrieval span, one unauthorized tool call, and a final answer with no policy citation. The final answer is fluent but not shippable.
The fix belongs in routing and approval gates, not sentence style.

items.text: List required and forbidden trace events.

blocks.title: Trace need
blocks.prompt: Why can final-answer scoring miss an agent failure?

options.text: Final answers never matter.
The agent may use wrong tools, skip evidence, or violate policy before writing plausible text.
Tools cannot affect users.

modules.title: Hard assertions guard contracts
modules.summary: Hard gates protect the workflow boundary.
objectives: Separate semantic scores from safety gates.

blocks.title: Contracts should not depend on judge vibes

spans.text: Hard assertions include valid schema, only allowed tools, required approval before side effects, expected source retrieved, timeout respected, and no forbidden network/file action.
Semantic scores can judge helpfulness or completeness after hard gates pass. A helpful answer with unauthorized tool use is still a release failure.
Put safety and contract assertions before LLM judges in the report.

blocks.analogy: A smoke detector does not ask whether the room feels cozy.

blocks.title: Hard gate
blocks.prompt: Which failure should block before semantic judging?

options.text: The answer used a synonym.
The agent called a forbidden external-send tool.
The response was one sentence shorter.

blocks.explanation: Safety contract failures are hard gates.

modules.title: Fixtures make agent runs repeatable
modules.sub: Agents need setup data, tool mocks, and baseline comparisons.
objectives: Label mock, recorded, and live tools.

blocks.title: Fixture design affects trust

spans.text: A workflow eval case should include user input, app state, documents, mock tool responses or sandboxed real tools, allowed resources, expected traces, and baseline run.
Tool mocks are useful but dangerous if they diverge from real tools. Keep contract tests against real adapters or recorded traces.
Every fixture should say whether it is mocked, recorded, or live.

blocks.analogy: Fixtures are the stage props that make the play repeatable.

spans.text: The case includes a customer with standard plan, a policy doc, a ticket ID, and a mock refund tool that records attempted calls. Expected trace: retrieve policy, draft explanation, no refund tool because approval is missing.
A separate integration test checks the real refund adapter schema.

items.text: Define allowed tools and expected traces.
Decide mock, recorded, or live tools.

blocks.title: Fixture risk
blocks.prompt: What is a risk of tool mocks?

options.text: They always make evals impossible.
They can hide integration bugs if they differ from real tool behavior.
They remove the need for expected traces.

modules.title: Trace assertions make path regressions testable
modules.sub: Required spans and forbidden tools can be checked in code.

blocks.title: Trace checks make invisible failures visible

spans.text: A trace assertion can be simple: expected retriever span exists, refund tool is absent, approval span appears before send, final schema is valid.
Use stable operation names and metadata. Assertions based on raw natural-language trace names will be brittle.
A missing parent span or tool span is a product signal, not just an observability issue.

blocks.analogy: Trace assertions are turnstiles in the workflow path.

blocks.title: Trace assertions for an agent run
blocks.code:
trace = [
    {"span": "router", "tool": None},
    {"span": "retrieval", "source": "refund_policy"},
    {"span": "draft_answer", "tool": None},
]
spans = {s["span"] for s in trace}
tools = {s.get("tool") for s in trace if s.get("tool")}
assert "retrieval" in spans
assert "send_refund" not in tools
assert "draft_answer" in spans
print("workflow trace OK")
blocks.explanation: The checker verifies required spans and forbidden tool use before semantic scoring.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Before reading the answer, predict whether the trace passes.
predictThenReveal.answer: It passes because retrieval and draft_answer exist and the forbidden send_refund tool is absent.

options.text: Testing for forbidden tools.
Using unstable operation names or missing metadata for important steps.
Checking required retrieval.

modules.title: Promote failures into regression cases
modules.sub: The suite should learn from escaped failures.
modules.summary: Agent eval is a feedback loop.

blocks.title: Incidents are future tests

spans.text: When a production trace shows an agent overusing tools, missing approval, or citing stale evidence, create the smallest case that would have caught it. Label severity and owner.
Track cost, latency, tool count, and pass rate by slice; a passing agent that takes 30 tool calls for a simple task can still regress.
The suite should answer “what changed?” after every prompt, model, KB, or tool update.

blocks.analogy: A good incident review leaves a tripwire behind.

blocks.title: Verify an agent workflow eval suite

spans.text: Review the suite against real runs.

items.text: Cases run the full production path or an intentionally faithful fixture.
Hard assertions cover schemas, tools, approvals, retrieval, and safety.
Semantic scores evaluate final task success with evidence.
Cost, latency, retries, and tool count compare to baseline.
Production incidents become minimal regression cases.

blocks.title: Regression loop
blocks.prompt: What should happen after a production agent incident?

options.text: Delete the trace.
Add a minimal eval case that would have caught the failure.
Trust manual demos only.

blocks.explanation: Agent eval suites learn from escaped failures.

eval.label: Eval
eval.laymanDefinition: A repeatable test of model or system behavior against expected criteria.
eval.technicalNote: In these lessons, evals are release evidence: they combine cases, assertions, scores, and review rules.

trace.label: Trace
trace.laymanDefinition: A structured record of one run, including spans, inputs, outputs, metadata, and scores.
trace.technicalNote: Traces make failures diagnosable by showing which retrieval, model, tool, or scoring step produced the result.

dataset.label: Dataset
dataset.laymanDefinition: A curated set of examples used for evaluation, debugging, or regression checks.
dataset.technicalNote: A useful eval dataset stores inputs, expected behavior, metadata slices, and source or rubric references.

judge.label: LLM-as-judge
judge.laymanDefinition: An LLM used to grade or compare outputs with a rubric.
judge.technicalNote: LLM judges are semantic scorers, not final authority; their prompts, model, thresholds, and spot checks must be versioned.

regression.label: Regression
regression.laymanDefinition: A previously working behavior that breaks after a prompt, model, data, or code change.
regression.technicalNote: Regression testing protects known capabilities and safety boundaries while allowing harmless wording variation.

rubric.label: Rubric
rubric.laymanDefinition: A scoring guide that states what a good answer or run must demonstrate.
rubric.technicalNote: Rubrics make qualitative judgment reviewable by naming criteria, severity, examples, and thresholds.

kb5.title: KB: Regression Testing for Agentic Systems

finalCheck.title: Knowledge check
finalCheck.intro: A quick check across the whole lesson — pick or type your answers.

questions.prompt: A customer-support agent always returns a polite, grammatically correct reply — but it sometimes calls a deprecated billing API mid-run. Which evaluation approach catches this failure that final-answer scoring alone would miss?

options.text: Increasing the semantic similarity threshold for the output text
Inspecting the trace for forbidden-tool calls during the run
Running more diverse user prompts in the test suite
Adding a human rater to score response quality

questions.explanation: Final-answer scoring only sees the output text; a forbidden-tool check on the trace catches illegal mid-run actions regardless of how good the final reply looks.

questions.prompt: Your eval suite includes a safety rule: 'The agent must never return a response that contains PII.' This rule should be implemented as a hard assertion rather than a semantic score. Why?

options.text: Semantic scores are too slow to compute for safety checks
Hard assertions produce a binary pass/fail that cannot be partially satisfied, making them suitable for non-negotiable contracts
Hard assertions are easier to write than semantic rubrics
Semantic scores cannot evaluate text that contains PII

questions.explanation: Hard assertions enforce a strict contract — a single violation is an outright failure — whereas a semantic score could award partial credit to a response that leaks PII, which is never acceptable.

questions.prompt: Describe the three fixture types used to make agent runs repeatable, and explain the key trade-off between them.
questions.acceptableAnswer: Mock tools return hardcoded responses and are fully deterministic but least realistic. Recorded tools replay captured real responses, balancing realism and repeatability. Live tools call real external services, giving the highest realism but introducing non-determinism and cost. The core trade-off is determinism and speed vs. real-world fidelity.
questions.explanation: Choosing a fixture type is always a trade-off: mocks give total control, recorded fixtures capture real behavior without live calls, and live tools maximize realism at the cost of stability and expense.

questions.prompt: You write a required-span check asserting that the span 'retrieve_policy_doc' must appear in every trace for a policy-lookup workflow. On the next run, the check fails. What does this tell you?

options.text: The agent's final answer was incorrect
The agent skipped or renamed a step that is mandatory for the workflow's correctness
A tool returned an unexpected data type
The latency of the run exceeded the baseline threshold

questions.explanation: A required-span check fails when an expected step is absent from the trace, signaling a path regression — the agent changed its execution route in a way that violates the workflow contract.

questions.prompt: A production incident reveals that the agent occasionally loops through a web-search tool six times before answering, doubling average latency. What is the BEST next step according to the 'promote failures into regression cases' practice?

options.text: Delete the web-search tool and replace it with a static knowledge base
Capture the incident trace as a fixture, add a latency-drift assertion and a max-tool-call check, assign it to an owner, and add it to the regression suite
Increase the latency budget in the SLA so the incident no longer counts as a failure
Re-run the same prompt 10 times and report the average latency as the new baseline

questions.explanation: Promoting an incident means turning it into a permanent regression case — preserving the trace as a fixture, adding drift and path assertions, and assigning ownership — so the same failure can never silently recur.
